1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
30	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
31	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
32	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
33	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
34	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
35	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
36	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
37	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
38	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
39	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
40	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
41	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
42	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
43	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
44	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
45	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
46	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
47	
48	## Requirements
49	
50	- Python 3.11 or newer
51	- no third-party runtime dependencies
52	
53	## Run the service
54	
55	```bash
56	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
57	```
58	
59	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
60	has bound the port.
61	
62	## HTTP API
63	
64	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
65	
66	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
67	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
68	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
69	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
70	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
71	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
72	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
73	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
74	
75	### Tenants and quotas
76	
77	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
78	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
79	and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
80	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
81	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
82	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
83	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
84	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
85	workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
86	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
87	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
88	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
89	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
90	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
91	
92	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
93	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
94	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status
95	queries, as well as the usage and bill queries. An empty
96	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
97	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
98	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
99	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
100	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
101	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
102	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
103	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
104	the usual `409 conflict`.
105	
106	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
107	hold:
108	
109	```http
110	PUT /quotas
111	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
112	X-Tenant-Id: acme
113	
114	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
115	```
116	
117	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
118	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
119	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
120	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
121	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
122	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
123	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
124	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
125	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
126	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
127	
128	```http
129	GET /quotas
130	X-Tenant-Id: acme
131	```
132	
133	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
134	when the tenant has declared none.
135	
136	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
137	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
138	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
139	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
140	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
141	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
142	
143	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
144	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
145	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
146	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
147	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
148	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
149	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
150	
151	### Usage metering and billing
152	
153	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
154	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
155	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
156	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
157	metered action types are:
158	
159	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
160	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
161	  definition;
162	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
163	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
164	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
165	  `schedule_triggered`;
166	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made. A
167	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
168	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
169	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails.
170	
171	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
172	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
173	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
174	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
175	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
176	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
177	
178	```http
179	GET /usage
180	X-Tenant-Id: acme
181	```
182	
183	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
184	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
185	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
186	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
187	
188	```http
189	GET /bill
190	X-Tenant-Id: acme
191	```
192	
193	Returns the per-type bill:
194	
195	```json
196	{"bill":{"items":[
197	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
198	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
199	],"total":2100}}
200	```
201	
202	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
203	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
204	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
205	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
206	
207	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
208	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
209	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
210	
211	### Health
212	
213	```http
214	GET /health
215	```
216	
217	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
218	
219	### Create a workflow
220	
221	```http
222	POST /workflows
223	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
224	
225	{
226	  "id": "order-flow",
227	  "nodes": [
228	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
229	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
230	  ]
231	}
232	```
233	
234	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
235	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
236	
237	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
238	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
239	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
240	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
241	
242	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
243	
244	```json
245	{
246	  "id": "order-flow",
247	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
248	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
249	}
250	```
251	
252	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
253	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
254	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
255	
256	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
257	
258	```json
259	{
260	  "id": "nightly-orders",
261	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
262	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
263	}
264	```
265	
266	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
267	
268	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
269	
270	```json
271	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
272	```
273	
274	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
275	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
276	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
277	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
278	`false`.
279	
280	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
281	
282	```json
283	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
284	```
285	
286	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
287	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
288	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
289	dependencies of its successors.
290	
291	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
292	
293	```json
294	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
295	```
296	
297	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
298	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
299	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
300	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
301	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
302	`retries_exhausted`.
303	
304	A task may instead declare an approval point:
305	
306	```json
307	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
308	```
309	
310	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
311	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
312	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
313	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
314	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
315	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
316	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
317	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
318	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
319	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
320	move the task.
321	
322	### Submit an approval decision
323	
324	```http
325	POST /executions/run-1/decision
326	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
327	
328	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
329	```
330	
331	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
332	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
333	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
334	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
335	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
336	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
337	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
338	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
339	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
340	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
341	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
342	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
343	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
344	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
345	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
346	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
347	404.
348	
349	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
350	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
351	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
352	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
353	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
354	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
355	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
356	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
357	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
358	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
359	shape and event stream.
360	
361	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
362	segment:
363	
364	```json
365	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
366	```
367	
368	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
369	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
370	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
371	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
372	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
373	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
374	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
375	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
376	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
377	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
378	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
379	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
380	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
381	loop node instead).
382	
383	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
384	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
385	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
386	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
387	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
388	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
389	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
390	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
391	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
392	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
393	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
394	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
395	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
396	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
397	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
398	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
399	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
400	belong only to their iterations.
401	
402	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
403	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
404	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
405	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
406	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
407	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
408	exactly.
409	
410	### Workflow versions
411	
412	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
413	
414	```json
415	{
416	  "id": "order-flow",
417	  "version": "2026-09-25",
418	  "nodes": [
419	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
420	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
421	  ]
422	}
423	```
424	
425	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
426	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
427	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
428	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
429	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
430	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
431	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
432	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
433	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
434	
435	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
436	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
437	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
438	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
439	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
440	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
441	
442	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
443	current version at the moment it starts:
444	
445	```http
446	POST /executions
447	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
448	
449	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
450	```
451	
452	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
453	
454	```json
455	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
456	```
457	
458	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
459	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
460	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
461	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
462	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
463	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
464	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
465	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
466	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
467	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
468	conclusions never change.
469	
470	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
471	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
472	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
473	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
474	stream with no added field.
475	
476	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
477	
478	```http
479	GET /workflows/order-flow
480	```
481	
482	```json
483	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
484	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
485	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
486	]}
487	```
488	
489	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
490	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
491	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
492	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
493	resources as usual.
494	
495	### Migrate a running execution to another version
496	
497	```http
498	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
499	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
500	
501	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
502	```
503	
504	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
505	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
506	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
507	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
508	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
509	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
510	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
511	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
512	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
513	carries the target version.
514	
515	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
516	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
517	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
518	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
519	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
520	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
521	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
522	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
523	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
524	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
525	
526	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
527	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
528	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
529	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
530	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
531	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
532	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
533	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
534	content.
535	
536	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
537	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
538	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
539	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
540	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
541	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
542	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
543	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
544	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
545	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
546	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
547	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
548	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
549	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
550	
551	### Start an execution
552	
553	```http
554	POST /executions
555	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
556	
557	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
558	```
559	
560	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
561	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
562	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
563	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
564	
565	An execution may declare a timeout:
566	
567	```json
568	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
569	```
570	
571	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
572	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
573	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
574	a timeout never expire.
575	
576	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
577	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
578	
579	```json
580	{
581	  "id": "run-3",
582	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
583	  "input": {},
584	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
585	}
586	```
587	
588	### Inspect an execution
589	
590	```http
591	GET /executions/run-1
592	GET /executions/run-1/events
593	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
594	```
595	
596	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
597	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
598	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
599	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
600	
601	### Webhook notifications
602	
603	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
604	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
605	
606	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
607	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
608	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
609	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
610	  reason);
611	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
612	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
613	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
614	
615	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
616	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
617	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
618	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
619	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
620	
621	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
622	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
623	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
624	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
625	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
626	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
627	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
628	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
629	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
630	triggered it.
631	
632	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
633	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
634	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
635	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
636	results as before.
637	
638	### Inspect the delivery history
639	
640	```http
641	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
642	```
643	
644	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
645	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
646	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
647	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
648	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
649	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
650	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
651	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
652	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
653	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
654	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
655	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
656	
657	### Schedules
658	
659	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
660	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
661	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
662	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
663	
664	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
665	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
666	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
667	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
668	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
669	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
670	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
671	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
672	
673	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
674	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
675	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
676	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
677	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
678	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
679	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
680	created is exposed through the status query below.
681	
682	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
683	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
684	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
685	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
686	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
687	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
688	
689	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
690	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
691	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
692	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
693	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
694	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
695	
696	### Declare or replace a schedule
697	
698	```http
699	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
700	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
701	
702	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
703	```
704	
705	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
706	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
707	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
708	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
709	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
710	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
711	
712	### Inspect the schedule status
713	
714	```http
715	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
716	```
717	
718	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
719	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
720	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
721	
722	```json
723	{
724	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
725	  "paused": false,
726	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
727	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
728	}
729	```
730	
731	The fields are:
732	
733	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
734	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
735	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
736	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
737	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
738	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
739	  `null` until the first period fires;
740	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
741	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
742	
743	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
744	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
745	
746	### Pause and resume a schedule
747	
748	```http
749	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
750	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
751	
752	{}
753	```
754	
755	```http
756	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
757	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
758	
759	{}
760	```
761	
762	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
763	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
764	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
765	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
766	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
767	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
768	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
769	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
770	
771	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
772	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
773	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
774	
775	### Checkpoints
776	
777	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
778	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
779	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
780	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
781	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
782	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
783	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
784	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
785	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
786	duplicating any node output.
787	
788	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
789	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
790	same state shape and event stream as before.
791	
792	### Complete the next ready node
793	
794	```http
795	POST /executions/run-1/advance
796	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
797	
798	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
799	```
800	
801	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
802	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
803	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
804	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
805	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
806	the status becomes `completed`.
807	
808	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
809	
810	```http
811	POST /executions/run-1/advance
812	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
813	
814	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
815	```
816	
817	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
818	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
819	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
820	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
821	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
822	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
823	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
824	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
825	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
826	
827	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
828	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
829	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
830	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
831	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
832	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
833	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
834	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
835	the execution stream.
836	
837	### Cancel an execution
838	
839	```http
840	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
841	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
842	```
843	
844	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
845	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
846	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
847	
848	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
849	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
850	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
851	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
852	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
853	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
854	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
855	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
856	
857	### Claim a work item
858	
859	```http
860	POST /executions/run-1/claim
861	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
862	
863	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
864	```
865	
866	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
867	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
868	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
869	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
870	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
871	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
872	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
873	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
874	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
875	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
876	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
877	
878	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
879	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
880	
881	```http
882	POST /executions/run-1/advance
883	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
884	
885	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
886	```
887	
888	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
889	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
890	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
891	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
892	an execution without any claim.
893	
894	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
895	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
896	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
897	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
898	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
899	
900	### Renew a lease
901	
902	```http
903	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
904	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
905	
906	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
907	```
908	
909	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
910	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
911	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
912	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
913	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
914	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
915	
916	### Release a work item
917	
918	```http
919	POST /executions/run-1/release
920	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
921	
922	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
923	```
924	
925	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
926	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
927	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
928	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
929	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
930	`not_found`.
931	
932	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
933	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
934	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
935	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
936	restarts.
937	
938	### Recover from a checkpoint
939	
940	```http
941	POST /executions/run-1/recover
942	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
943	
944	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
945	```
946	
947	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
948	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
949	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
950	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
951	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
952	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
953	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
954	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
955	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
956	execution state and events.
957	
958	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
959	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
960	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
961	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
962	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
963	stays consistent with the materialized state.
964	
965	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
966	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
967	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
968	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
969	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
970	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
971	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
972	
973	### Replay
974	
975	```http
976	POST /executions/run-1/replay
977	```
978	
979	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
980	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
981	and the rebuilt execution.
982	
983	## Errors
984	
985	Errors use this shape:
986	
987	```json
988	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
989	```
990	
991	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
992	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
993	declarations and the usage and bill queries require a tenant, and quota
994	limits are positive integers validated by the
995	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
996	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
997	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
998	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
999	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
1000	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
1001	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
1002	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
1003	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
1004	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
1005	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
1006	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
1007	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
1008	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
1009	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
1010	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
1011	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
1012	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
1013	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1014	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
1015	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
1016	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
1017	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
1018	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
1019	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
1020	A decision by an approver who is
1021	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
1022	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
1023	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
1024	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
1025	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
1026	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
1027	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
1028	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
1029	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
1030	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
1031	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
1032	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
1033	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
1034	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
1035	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
1036	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
1037	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
1038	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
1039	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
1040	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
1041	
1042	## Tests
1043	
1044	```bash
1045	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
1046	```
1047	
1048
